solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap here is List I item D — 'deposits in State Cooperative Banks registered with DICGC.' Students who carry the general exclusion of 'government deposits' and conflate 'State cooperative' with 'State government' will incorrectly mark these as excluded. State Cooperative Banks are cooperative banking institutions eligible for DICGC coverage — they are not government deposits.
solution.final_explanation:
This question tests whether students can correctly classify deposit categories and bank types under DICGC's coverage framework.

Correct pairings:
• A (Recurring deposits) – 2 (Covered under DICGC): Recurring deposits are standard retail deposits explicitly within DICGC's coverage — same as savings, fixed, and current deposits.
• B (Deposits of foreign governments with Indian banks) – 4 (Excluded from DICGC coverage): Foreign government deposits are among the explicitly excluded categories.
• C (Inter-bank deposits) – 3 (Excluded to prevent circular insurance): If Bank X deposits with Bank Y and both Y's deposits are insured, Y's failure would trigger Bank X's insurance claim — a circular and potentially destabilising outcome. Hence excluded.
• D (Deposits in State Cooperative Banks registered with DICGC) – 1 (Covered if bank is registered member): State Cooperative Banks are eligible cooperative banks — not government entities. Their deposits are covered once the bank registers with DICGC.

Trap pairing: D-4 is the most dangerous error — conflating 'State Cooperative Bank' with 'State Government deposit.'

Value Addition:
• The inter-bank deposit exclusion is a systemic risk management choice — it prevents domino-effect insurance claims during banking system stress.
• State Cooperative Banks sit above District Central Cooperative Banks in the short-term cooperative credit structure.
• Foreign bank branches in India are covered; foreign GOVERNMENT deposits are not — the entity making the deposit, not the bank receiving it, determines exclusion.

solution.concept_anchor: Moral hazard mitigants in deposit insurance design

statement_analysis.statement: Risk-based premiums, under which banks with riskier portfolios pay higher insurance premiums, are considered a mechanism to reduce the bank-side moral hazard created by deposit insurance.
statement_analysis.reason: Risk-based premiums impose a direct cost on risky behaviour — banks taking excessive risks pay more for insurance, internalising part of the risk externality created by deposit insurance.

statement_analysis.statement: Full deposit insurance coverage — covering 100% of all deposits without any limit — is the most effective way to prevent bank runs and is therefore the preferred design in most advanced economies.
statement_analysis.reason: Full coverage maximises moral hazard — both depositors (no monitoring incentive) and banks (no discipline from depositors). Most advanced economies deliberately set coverage limits to preserve partial market discipline; unlimited coverage is not the preferred design.

statement_analysis.statement: Co-insurance arrangements, where depositors bear a percentage of any loss, are considered a mitigant to depositor-side moral hazard in deposit insurance design.
statement_analysis.reason: Co-insurance preserves some 'skin in the game' for depositors — if they bear a portion of losses, they retain an incentive to monitor their bank's health, reducing complacency.

solution.strong_distractor: b — This is the correct answer here. The strong distractor FOR STUDENTS is Statement 2, which sounds authoritative ('full coverage → maximum stability') and could mislead students into thinking it is correct.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: risk-based premiums as a moral hazard mitigant — this is a standard policy mechanism. Statement 1 is Correct — not the NOT-correct answer.

Evaluate Statement 2: 'full coverage is preferred in most advanced economies' — this inverts the policy reality. Advanced economies deliberately limit coverage to preserve market discipline. Full coverage creates maximum moral hazard. Statement 2 is NOT correct.
Evaluate Statement 3: co-insurance as mitigant to depositor moral hazard — correct in design theory. Statement 3 is Correct.
Only Statement 2 is NOT correct — answer is (b) 2 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 uses a reversed-causation argument: 'full coverage best prevents bank runs (stability goal) → therefore preferred.' The flaw is that while full coverage does maximally prevent bank runs, it simultaneously maximises moral hazard — an unacceptable trade-off that makes full coverage unpopular among policymakers. The statement presents only one side of the design equation. Advanced economies balance stability against moral hazard, which is why all major deposit insurance schemes have coverage limits.
solution.final_explanation:
Deposit insurance design involves deliberate trade-offs between stability (preventing bank runs) and market discipline (limiting moral hazard).

• Statement 1 — Correct: Risk-based premiums are the primary tool to address bank-side moral hazard. By charging riskier banks more, they introduce a cost to excessive risk-taking within the insured framework. The FDIC (USA) uses risk-based premiums; India's DICGC uses a flat rate.
• Statement 2 — NOT Correct: Full deposit insurance without a coverage limit would maximise the prevention of bank runs but would eliminate all depositor incentive to monitor banks and remove any market discipline on bank risk-taking. This combination of problems makes unlimited coverage economically unsound. Most advanced economies deliberately cap coverage.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Co-insurance (e.g., depositor bears 10% of any loss) preserves depositor vigilance. Though not currently used in India, it is a theoretically sound mitigant to depositor-side moral hazard.

Value Addition:
• India's ₹5 lakh limit is a deliberate design: small depositors get full protection (financial inclusion); large depositors bear partial risk (market discipline).
• The Financial Stability Board (FSB) and IADI guidelines discourage unlimited deposit insurance except as a temporary crisis-management measure.
• During the 2008 global financial crisis, some countries temporarily introduced unlimited guarantees — but only as emergency measures, not permanent design.

solution.concept_anchor: Payment Bank deposit ceiling fully within DICGC coverage limit
solution.strong_distractor: c — Students who know 'Small Finance Banks are covered' may select (c) without verifying whether the 'savings deposits only' qualifier is accurate — it is not; SFBs cover all standard deposit types.
elimination_logic: Evaluate (a): Payment Banks have a ₹2 lakh deposit ceiling per customer; DICGC limit is ₹5 lakh — since ₹2 lakh < ₹5 lakh, all Payment Bank depositors are 100% covered. This pair is correctly matched.

Evaluate (b): Small Finance Banks' DICGC coverage is mandatory since they are licensed commercial banks — but the pair claims coverage requires 'prior RBI approval' separately, which is not accurate. Coverage is automatic upon licensing. Incorrectly matched.
Evaluate (c): SFBs are covered for ALL standard deposits (savings, fixed, current, recurring) — not just savings deposits. The 'savings deposits only' restriction is fabricated. Incorrect.

Evaluate (d): Payment Banks are covered regardless of whether deposits are in savings or current accounts — the ₹2 lakh ceiling applies to the total deposits, not just savings. The pair incorrectly states current account deposits are excluded. Incorrect.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (c) uses a 'savings deposits only' qualifier for Small Finance Banks — a plausible-sounding restriction since SFBs were initially positioned as serving rural/semi-urban savings needs. In reality, SFBs as licensed commercial banks can offer all deposit types and all are covered under DICGC. The conflation trap merges 'SFB's target customer base (small savers)' with 'SFB's DICGC coverage scope,' which are unrelated.
solution.final_explanation:
Newer banking categories (Payment Banks, Small Finance Banks) and their DICGC coverage are high-value examination topics.

• Option (a) — Correctly matched: Payment Banks are licensed commercial banks covered under DICGC. Their ₹2 lakh per-customer deposit ceiling means every depositor's entire balance is automatically within the ₹5 lakh DICGC limit. 100% coverage for all Payment Bank depositors is structurally guaranteed.
• Option (b) — Incorrectly matched: Small Finance Banks automatically acquire DICGC coverage as part of their commercial bank licensing — no separate prior RBI approval for DICGC registration is required as a distinct step.
• Option (c) — Incorrectly matched: SFBs are covered for all standard deposit types — savings, fixed, current, and recurring. Restricting coverage to 'savings deposits only' is factually wrong.
• Option (d) — Incorrectly matched: Payment Banks can offer both savings and current accounts (within the ₹2 lakh ceiling) and both are covered under DICGC.

Value Addition:
• Payment Banks' 100% DICGC coverage is a significant credibility feature for financial inclusion outreach.
• SFBs were created precisely to serve underserved segments — their full DICGC coverage supports depositor confidence in these institutions.
• Both SFBs and Payment Banks are subject to the same ₹5 lakh per-depositor-per-bank ceiling as any other commercial bank.

solution.concept_anchor: DICGC name includes credit guarantee but primary function is deposit insurance
elimination_logic: Step 1 — Is A correct? Yes. DICGC's primary active function today is deposit insurance — its credit guarantee activities have been substantially wound down or transferred to other entities.

Step 2 — Is R correct? No. CGTMSE was not established as a result of DICGC's credit guarantee wind-down. CGTMSE was set up in 2000 as a joint initiative of the Ministry of MSME and SIDBI — it has its own independent origin and mandate, not born out of DICGC's transition.
Step 3: Since R is factually incorrect, the answer is (c) — A is correct but R is incorrect.
Confirm: correct_option is (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: This is an entity-swap trap in the Reason. CGTMSE (Credit Guarantee Fund Trust for Micro and Small Enterprises) was established in 2000 by the Ministry of MSME and SIDBI — not as a successor to DICGC's credit guarantee functions. R incorrectly establishes a causal lineage between DICGC's wind-down and CGTMSE's creation. Students who know both DICGC wound down credit guarantee AND CGTMSE exists may connect the dots incorrectly without knowing CGTMSE's independent origin.
solution.final_explanation:
DICGC's institutional evolution involves a shift from dual functions to a predominantly deposit insurance focus.

Assertion (A) — Correct: While DICGC's full name includes 'Credit Guarantee,' its credit guarantee schemes (for small industries, small traders, etc.) have been largely wound down or transferred over time. Today, deposit insurance is DICGC's primary active function — the 'Credit Guarantee' in its name reflects historical mandate, not current operational focus.

Reason (R) — Incorrect: CGTMSE was established in August 2000 as a joint initiative of the Government of India (Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises) and SIDBI — not as a successor institution to DICGC's credit guarantee operations. CGTMSE has its own legislative and institutional foundation, independent of DICGC's evolution.

Since A is correct and R is factually wrong, the correct option is (c).

Value Addition:
• CGTMSE provides collateral-free credit guarantees to MSEs through Member Lending Institutions — a distinct product from what DICGC historically offered.
• DICGC's remaining credit guarantee operations (if any) are minimal — the active credit guarantee ecosystem in India is led by CGTMSE, NCGTC, and sector-specific guarantee trusts.
• The name 'DICGC' is now somewhat misleading — it suggests equal weight to both functions, whereas deposit insurance dominates current operations.

solution.concept_anchor: De-registration cuts coverage only for post-de-registration deposits
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who assume de-registration 'cancels' all insurance will choose (b), failing to account for the temporal protection of pre-de-registration deposits.
elimination_logic: Identify the key facts: Bank Y was de-registered in March 2023. Sunita made deposits in January 2023 (before de-registration) and June 2023 (after de-registration). Bank failed in December 2023.
Apply the de-registration rule: deposits made BEFORE de-registration date retain insurance; deposits made AFTER de-registration are uninsured.
Sunita's January 2023 deposit (₹2 lakh): made while Bank Y was a DICGC member — covered up to ₹5 lakh.
Sunita's June 2023 deposit (₹1.5 lakh): made after de-registration — not covered. Total DICGC payout: ₹2 lakh. Answer: (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: This is a temporal-swap trap: two deposits, one before and one after de-registration. Students who apply 'de-registration cancels all coverage' will pick (b) (no coverage at all). Students who apply 'de-registration doesn't matter, she's covered' will pick (a) (₹3.5 lakh total). The precise rule — temporal cut-off at de-registration date — is needed to correctly isolate the covered portion. The trap works because both extreme answers (full coverage and no coverage) are available as options.
solution.final_explanation:
De-registration from DICGC creates a temporal threshold with precise consequences for depositor protection.

Applicable principle: De-registration date is the cut-off. Deposits made while the bank was a DICGC member retain their insurance. Deposits made after de-registration are not covered — the insurance contract for each deposit is formed at the time of deposit, contingent on the bank's membership status at that moment.

Mapping to scenario:
• January 2023 deposit (₹2 lakh): Bank Y was a DICGC member — this deposit is insured. Full ₹2 lakh is recoverable from DICGC.
• June 2023 deposit (₹1.5 lakh): Bank Y had already been de-registered in March 2023 — this deposit has no DICGC coverage. Sunita must seek recovery from the liquidation estate for this amount.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Applies full coverage to both deposits — ignores the de-registration cut-off.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: Applies no coverage to either deposit — incorrectly treats de-registration as retroactive.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Covers the June deposit (post-de-registration) which is wrong; excludes the January deposit incorrectly.
• Option (d) — Correct: Only the January 2023 deposit (₹2 lakh) is covered — made before de-registration. Total DICGC payout: ₹2 lakh.

Value Addition:
• A bank can be de-registered while still operating — depositors of an operational bank may unknowingly be uninsured.
• RBI's DICGC registration list is publicly available — depositors can verify their bank's status.
• The de-registration mechanism acts as a compliance incentive: banks risk losing depositor trust if de-registered.

solution.concept_anchor: India covers 98% accounts but only 50% deposit value — distinction critical

statement_analysis.statement: India's deposit insurance scheme, with a ₹5 lakh coverage limit, covers approximately 98% of all depositor accounts by number, though the percentage of total deposit value insured is significantly lower.
statement_analysis.reason: The ~98% figure refers to the proportion of accounts (by count) where the entire balance is within ₹5 lakh — since most Indian depositors hold small balances. However, by deposit value (rupee amount), only about 50% of total deposits are covered — because large corporate/institutional deposits are uncapped and far exceed ₹5 lakh.

statement_analysis.statement: India's Deposit Insurance Fund (DIF) reserve ratio — the proportion of insured deposits covered by the fund balance — is higher than the FDIC's Designated Reserve Ratio of 1.35%, indicating superior fund adequacy.
statement_analysis.reason: India's DIF reserve ratio is generally lower than international benchmarks, including the FDIC's 1.35% DRR — not higher. India's DIF adequacy is a concern, particularly for simultaneous multiple-bank failure scenarios.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who recall 'India now covers 98% of depositors' and assume 'DIF is large because premiums are high' may accept both statements as correct without knowing the specific DRR comparison.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: 98% by account count but ~50% by deposit value — this is a well-established distinction in DICGC policy discussion. Statement 1 is Correct.

Evaluate Statement 2: India's DIF reserve ratio is NOT higher than FDIC's 1.35% DRR — India's ratio is lower, not higher, raising adequacy concerns. 'Higher than FDIC' is the false claim. Statement 2 is Incorrect.
Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect — answer is (c) Statement 1 correct but Statement 2 incorrect.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 is a partial-truth trap: the DIF reserve ratio concept is real, the FDIC's 1.35% figure is accurate, but the comparative direction ('India higher than FDIC') is inverted. Students who know India 'recently strengthened DICGC' through the 2020 coverage enhancement and 2021 Amendment may assume fund adequacy also improved beyond FDIC standards — a logical but factually unsupported inference. India's DIF remains below international benchmarks for reserve adequacy.
solution.final_explanation:
Distinguishing coverage breadth (by account count) from coverage depth (by deposit value) is one of DICGC's most examined analytical concepts.

• Statement 1 — Correct: India's ₹5 lakh limit covers nearly all small depositors in full (98% of accounts) — because most Indians hold modest bank balances. However, wealthy individuals and large corporates hold disproportionately large deposits that far exceed ₹5 lakh, so by rupee value only about 50% of total deposits are covered. This is the fundamental policy tension in deposit insurance design.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: India's DIF reserve ratio (DIF balance as % of insured deposits) is lower than the FDIC's Designated Reserve Ratio of 1.35% — not higher. A lower reserve ratio means the fund is less able to absorb large-scale simultaneous failures. This is a known systemic vulnerability in India's deposit insurance architecture.

Value Addition:
• The FDIC's 1.35% DRR is a statutory target — if it falls below this, the FDIC must implement a restoration plan.
• India has no equivalent statutory DIF target ratio — the adequacy is assessed periodically without a legislated floor.
• Improving India's DIF reserve ratio would require either higher premiums, a government capital injection, or both — a continuing policy debate.

solution.strong_distractor: b — 10 paise per ₹100 is the immediately preceding premium rate (before the 2020 revision) — students who recall 'the old rate' without knowing it was revised will pick this.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (b): 10 paise per ₹100 was the rate BEFORE the 2020 revision — it is the immediately preceding rate, making it the strongest distractor.

solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (b) (10 paise) is the pre-2020 rate — the temporal-swap trap. Students who memorised DICGC's premium rate at some point before 2020 will recall '10 paise' and mark (b). The 2020 revision increased the rate from 10 to 12 paise — a 20% increase that accompanied the coverage enhancement to ₹5 lakh. Both changes (coverage and premium) were part of the same 2020 reform package.
solution.final_explanation:
DICGC's premium structure is a flat-rate system applied annually to assessable deposits.

• Option (a) — Correct: 12 paise per ₹100 of assessable deposits per annum is the current premium rate, effective from 2020. This rate was revised upward from the previous 10 paise per ₹100.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: 10 paise per ₹100 was the rate before the 2020 revision — this is the immediately preceding rate and the primary trap for students who memorised the pre-2020 figure.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: 5 paise per ₹100 has no association with DICGC's premium history.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: 15 paise per ₹100 exceeds the current rate — not the applicable premium.

Value Addition:
• The 2020 changes were simultaneous: coverage limit raised from ₹1 lakh to ₹5 lakh AND premium rate raised from 10 paise to 12 paise — connecting both for memory.
• Premium is borne by banks — depositors do not directly pay it, though it may be implicitly reflected in deposit interest rate spreads.
• Premium is calculated on assessable deposits (the total insurable pool), not just the ₹5 lakh-capped insured deposits — a distinction that makes the premium base larger than the insurance liability.

solution.concept_anchor: PMC Bank crisis intersection with cooperative bank oversight and DICGC reform

statement_analysis.statement: The Punjab & Maharashtra Co-operative Bank (PMC) crisis exposed weaknesses in the pre-2021 DICGC framework, specifically the requirement for depositors to wait for full winding-up proceedings before receiving insurance payments.
statement_analysis.reason: PMC Bank was placed under RBI's restrictive Directions from September 2019, and depositors faced years of uncertain waiting under the pre-2021 framework — this directly catalysed the 2021 DICGC Amendment.

statement_analysis.statement: The DICGC (Amendment) Act, 2021 also extended deposit insurance coverage to Primary Agricultural Credit Societies (PACS) operating in rural areas, addressing the cooperative sector gap highlighted by the PMC crisis.
statement_analysis.reason: The 2021 Amendment reformed payment timing for existing DICGC-covered entities — it did NOT extend coverage to PACS. PACS remain outside DICGC's ambit even after the 2021 Amendment.

statement_analysis.statement: Multi-state cooperative societies in India are regulated by the Central Government, while single-state cooperative societies fall under state government jurisdiction — a dual regulatory structure that complicates uniform deposit insurance coverage for the cooperative sector.
statement_analysis.reason: This jurisdictional complexity is a genuine structural barrier to extending DICGC coverage uniformly across all cooperative entities — a policy gap that the 2021 Amendment did not address.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Students who know the 2021 Amendment was 'about cooperative banks' (it was contextualised by a cooperative bank crisis) may assume Statement 2 is true — that it extended coverage to PACS.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: PMC Bank crisis as the proximate trigger for the 2021 DICGC Amendment — this is factually established. Statement 1 is Correct.

Evaluate Statement 2: '2021 Amendment extended coverage to PACS' — false. The Amendment addressed payment timing, not coverage extension to new entity types. PACS remain uncovered. Statement 2 is Incorrect.

Evaluate Statement 3: multi-state vs. single-state cooperative jurisdictional split — this is a genuine constitutional and regulatory feature complicating cooperative sector insurance. Statement 3 is Correct.
Statements 1 and 3 correct; Statement 2 incorrect — answer is (c) 1 and 3 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 exploits the PMC-Bank-as-cooperative-bank narrative. Since PMC Bank was a cooperative bank and the 2021 Amendment was motivated by the PMC crisis, students may assume the Amendment addressed the broader cooperative coverage gap. It did not — the 2021 Amendment's scope was limited to payment timing mechanics for already-covered entities. PACS coverage would require a separate legislative effort involving both central and state jurisdictions.
solution.final_explanation:
The PMC Bank crisis was the political trigger for the 2021 Amendment, but understanding precisely what the Amendment did and did not do is critical.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Before 2021, PMC Bank depositors waited years because payment required completed liquidation proceedings. Their ordeal directly drove the legislative push for time-bound payments. The 2021 Amendment addressed this exact gap.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The 2021 Amendment reformed when existing insured entities' depositors receive payment (within 90 days of moratorium). It did not extend the universe of covered entities. PACS remain excluded — the cooperative society vs. cooperative bank distinction was not altered by the Amendment.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The constitutional division of regulatory authority — Centre for multi-state cooperatives, States for single-state cooperatives — creates a fragmented oversight landscape. Extending DICGC (a central institution) to state-regulated cooperatives raises jurisdictional questions requiring legislative coordination.

Value Addition:
• PMC Bank had assets of over ₹11,000 crore — not a small institution. Its crisis affected thousands of depositors and preceded the 2021 reform.
• RBI's expanded powers over cooperative banks (via the Banking Regulation Amendment Act, 2020) addressed some governance gaps but not deposit insurance coverage.
• The PACS coverage gap affects millions of rural depositors who rely on PACS for savings — a significant financial inclusion concern.

solution.concept_anchor: Categories excluded from DICGC deposit insurance coverage
solution.strong_distractor: c — Inter-bank deposits are commonly associated with regular banking operations, and students may assume they are covered because 'banks also need protection.' The exclusion is specific and policy-driven.
elimination_logic: Identify the category: the question asks which deposit type IS covered by DICGC — the odd one out is the type that DOES NOT share the 'excluded' attribute.
Option (a) — State government deposits: excluded from DICGC coverage.
Option (b) — Recurring deposits of resident individuals: COVERED by DICGC — this is the odd one out among a list of excluded items.
Option (c) — Inter-bank deposits: excluded from DICGC coverage.
Option (d) — Deposits of foreign governments: excluded from DICGC coverage. Answer: (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The question inverts the usual framing — asking what IS covered among mostly excluded items. Students on autopilot who mark 'which is NOT covered' will pick (b) thinking it is the exception from coverage. The odd-one-out here is the one deposit type that enjoys DICGC coverage — recurring deposits of resident individuals — while all others are among the standard exclusion categories.
solution.final_explanation:
DICGC's exclusion list is well-defined and this question tests whether students can identify the one item that does NOT belong to it.

• Option (a) — State government deposits: Excluded. Both Central and State government deposits are outside DICGC's coverage net.
• Option (b) — Recurring deposits of resident individuals: COVERED under DICGC — the odd one out. This is a standard retail deposit type within DICGC's protection. All other options belong to the exclusion list.
• Option (c) — Inter-bank deposits: Excluded to prevent circular insurance claims — if Bank A deposits with Bank B and both are insured, Bank B's failure would trigger Bank A's insurance claim, creating systemic feedback loops.
• Option (d) — Deposits of foreign governments: Excluded alongside Central and State government deposits — sovereign entities are not the intended beneficiaries of retail deposit insurance.

Value Addition:
• The exclusion list is designed to focus DICGC's protection on retail depositors — individuals, small businesses, and trusts.
• Deposits held outside India (even in Indian banks' overseas branches) are also excluded.
• Deposits specifically exempted by RBI with DICGC concurrence form a residual exclusion category allowing regulatory flexibility.

statement_analysis.statement: The Financial Resolution and Deposit Insurance Bill, 2017 proposed the establishment of a Resolution Corporation to oversee the resolution of financial firms, which would have superseded DICGC's role.
statement_analysis.reason: The FRDI Bill proposed a Resolution Corporation with comprehensive resolution powers over banks, insurance companies, and other financial entities — this would have subsumed DICGC's deposit insurance function within a broader resolution framework.

statement_analysis.statement: The 'bail-in' provision in the FRDI Bill, 2017 would have allowed a failing financial institution to use depositor funds beyond the insured limit to finance its own resolution, which was a key reason for the Bill's withdrawal.
statement_analysis.reason: The bail-in clause — allowing a failing bank to convert uninsured depositor deposits into equity or haircut them — generated massive public opposition. This was the primary reason the Bill was withdrawn in 2018.

statement_analysis.statement: After the withdrawal of the FRDI Bill, the Government of India enacted the Banking Resolution Act, 2019 as an alternative framework, which retained certain elements of the bail-in concept in a modified form.
statement_analysis.reason: No 'Banking Resolution Act, 2019' was enacted. The FRDI Bill was withdrawn and no direct replacement legislation was passed — the response was instead the strengthening of the existing DICGC framework through the 2021 Amendment.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) presents Statements 1 and 3 together. Since Statement 3 sounds authoritative (a named act in a plausible year), students who accept Statements 1 and 3 as correct without verifying Statement 3's existence will pick this option.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: FRDI proposed a Resolution Corporation to supersede DICGC — this is a core feature of the Bill. Statement 1 is Correct.
Evaluate Statement 2: bail-in clause causing public outrage and the Bill's withdrawal — this is the documented historical record. Statement 2 is Correct.

Evaluate Statement 3: 'Banking Resolution Act, 2019' — this is a fabricated legislation. No such act exists. After FRDI's withdrawal, the actual reform was the DICGC Amendment Act, 2021. Statement 3 is Incorrect.
Statements 1 and 2 correct; Statement 3 incorrect — answer is (d) 1 and 2 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 is a plausible-fabrication trap — a named act (Banking Resolution Act) in a plausible year (2019, between FRDI withdrawal and DICGC Amendment). Students who do not specifically know that no such act was passed will find it credible. The UPSC frequently tests whether students know what did NOT happen as much as what did. The actual post-FRDI reform was the DICGC Amendment Act, 2021 — not a separate resolution legislation.
solution.final_explanation:
The FRDI Bill episode and its aftermath are an important case study in banking regulation policy evolution.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The FRDI Bill proposed a single Resolution Corporation with powers over all financial sector firms. For banks, this would have replaced DICGC as the primary deposit protection mechanism — a comprehensive structural overhaul.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The bail-in clause (Section 52 of the FRDI Bill) specified that a failing institution could use depositor funds (beyond the insured amount) for its own rescue — effectively making depositors unsecured creditors who could lose part of their deposits in a resolution. This triggered widespread public alarm and social media campaigns, leading to the Bill's withdrawal in August 2018.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: No 'Banking Resolution Act, 2019' exists. This is a fabricated legislation. Post-withdrawal of FRDI, no comprehensive resolution framework was enacted. The Government instead strengthened the DICGC framework through the 2021 Amendment — a much narrower but practically important reform.

Value Addition:
• The FRDI Bill would have been India's first comprehensive bank resolution legislation — its absence means bank resolution still relies on ad hoc RBI regulatory actions.
• The bail-in debate remains relevant globally — bail-in tools are used in the EU's Bank Recovery and Resolution Directive (BRRD).
• India currently lacks a formal cross-sector resolution mechanism for financial firms — a gap in regulatory architecture.

solution.concept_anchor: Depositor retains right to claim uninsured balance from liquidation estate
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who understand 'DICGC steps into depositor's shoes' may extend this to conclude that DICGC takes over ALL claims, eliminating the depositor's right to the uninsured portion.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (b): subrogation is limited to the amount DICGC paid (₹5 lakh) — it does not extinguish the depositor's claim for the uninsured ₹3 lakh. The depositor retains an independent creditor status for the excess.
Eliminate (c): DICGC subrogation operates automatically by law — it does not require a formal court petition from the depositor to transfer rights.
Eliminate (d): both DICGC (subrogated creditor for ₹5 lakh) and the depositor (remaining creditor for ₹3 lakh) can participate in liquidation — they are not mutually exclusive creditors.
Confirm (a): DICGC pays ₹5 lakh and becomes a subrogated creditor for that amount; the depositor retains an independent claim against the liquidation estate for the remaining ₹3 lakh.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap: students who know 'DICGC steps into depositor's shoes through subrogation' extend this to 'DICGC steps into ALL of the depositor's shoes, eliminating the depositor's own claim.' Subrogation is bounded — it applies only to the amount actually paid by DICGC. The depositor's rights beyond the insured amount (₹3 lakh in this case) remain with the depositor, not DICGC. Confusing partial subrogation with complete assignment of all creditor rights is the specific knowledge gap this question targets.
solution.final_explanation:
Understanding the precise boundaries of subrogation is essential for both examination and practical depositor protection analysis.

• Option (a) — Correct: When a bank fails and a depositor holds ₹8 lakh, DICGC pays ₹5 lakh and becomes subrogated to that extent — it steps into the depositor's shoes as a creditor of the failed bank for ₹5 lakh. The depositor retains an independent right to claim the remaining ₹3 lakh (uninsured portion) from the liquidation estate.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: Subrogation does not transfer the depositor's entire claim to DICGC. The assignment is limited to the insured amount paid. The depositor and DICGC become simultaneous but separately quantified creditors in the liquidation.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Subrogation is a legal mechanism that operates automatically when DICGC pays the insured amount — no separate court petition is required from the depositor to effect the transfer.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Both DICGC (for ₹5 lakh) and the depositor (for ₹3 lakh) participate in the same liquidation proceedings as independent creditors. Their claims are additive, not mutually exclusive.

Value Addition:
• In practice, recoveries from failed bank liquidation estates are low — both DICGC and the uninsured depositor face uncertain and typically partial recovery.
• Under the 2021 Amendment, subrogation is formalised at the moratorium stage — depositors receiving payment during moratorium must formally assign their claim rights.
• Depositors with balances above ₹5 lakh should not assume the uninsured portion is lost — they are creditors and can participate in liquidation distribution.
